Read text file `/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/README.md`.
1|# MobileMoE-S on vLLM Metal: where does the memory bandwidth go?
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|An indie-track project for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).
6|
7|**The question:** when vLLM serves Meta's on-device MobileMoE-S model on an Apple M1 Pro, how much of the GPU's memory bandwidth does it actually use, where does the remaining time go, and which fixes turn unused bandwidth into more tokens per second?
8|
9|Each measured decode step is plotted against two limits: peak bandwidth (~200 GB/s) and peak compute (~5.2 TFLOPS). One request at a time should be limited by bandwidth. Running more requests per step reuses the weights already read, until compute becomes the limit. In a mixture-of-experts model, each extra request may also pull in different experts, so the bytes read grow too. Terms are defined in [GLOSSARY.md](claude/GLOSSARY.md).
10|
11|**Status:** the baseline is measured ([results below](#baseline-results)). vLLM serves MobileMoE-S at 12–17% of the GPU's peak memory bandwidth, and each decode step takes 6–8 times longer than the bandwidth and compute limits require. Microbenchmarks show where the time goes ([claude/findings/decode-bottlenecks.md](claude/findings/decode-bottlenecks.md)):
12|
13|- about 870 small GPU kernels per step, each with a fixed cost;
14|- expert weights read once per (token, expert) pair;
15|- attention reading each key/value head three times.
16|
17|A piece-by-piece measurement inside the real step, in vLLM and plain MLX side by side, is in [claude/findings/step-breakdown.md](claude/findings/step-breakdown.md):
18|- vLLM's scheduler and runner are small, 0.5–1.6 ms per step.
19|- vLLM's extra 7–20% over plain MLX is in vllm-metal's attention path.
20|- With one request, the mixture-of-experts block's routing and combine cost more than its expert products. With 32 requests, the routed experts take half the step.
21|- Piece by piece, only the output layer gets near peak bandwidth (about 160 GB/s with one request).
22|- The GPU's own counters, recorded with Xcode, show the GPU busy 92–98% of the time at only 17–28% of peak bandwidth, with most of its thread slots empty.
23|  - With one request each weight is read once.
24|  - With 32 requests a step reads about twice what the model needs: the routed experts read 908 MB from memory for 443 MB of weights. MLX's split quantized products also write about 170 MB of partial sums per step.
25|
26|[claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md](claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md) explains where the bottleneck is in plain English, with each number worked through from its inputs.
27|
28|Next: Muse Spark, working in Muse Code, Meta's own coding agent, diagnoses the bottlenecks from these findings with helper agents and writes GPU kernels against them. An independent grader checks them ([ADR 0006](claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)).
29|
30|## How Meta's models are used
31|
32|- **MobileMoE-S** (open weights) is the model under study, served by vLLM through vllm-metal. The baseline serves the int4 `facebook/MobileMoE-S-QAT` ([why](claude/adr/0002-int4-qat-baseline.md)); the bfloat16 `facebook/MobileMoE-S-SFT` is used to check the port.
33|- **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`; Meta Model API) works in **Muse Code**, Meta's own coding agent, started only with `tools/muse-agent/start.sh`.
34|  - Each round follows the skill [.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md](.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md). Muse's helper agents investigate the findings and the code; it writes a diagnosis, chooses which bottleneck to attack, writes fused GPU kernels, and runs the grader on them itself.
35|  - Its work goes to `muse-spark/` on the branch `muse-agent`, with the transcripts of its sessions. Its task was committed and tagged `agent-era` ([brief](claude/muse-agent-brief.md)); the move to Muse Code and the skill were committed and tagged `muse-code-era` before its first Muse Code session.
36|
37|## Who made what
38|
39|Every commit is made by **surucuonur**. The co-author on each commit shows whose work it holds:
40|
41|| Who | What | Where |
42||---|---|---|
43|| **surucuonur** | Direction, decisions, running the machine, starting the Muse Spark sessions | every commit |
44|| **Claude Code** (Claude Opus 5.5) | Benchmark, grader and provenance code, measurements, write-ups, Muse Spark's brief and round skill | `bench/`, `claude/`, `tools/`, `.agents/skills/`, this README. Commits co-authored by `claude`. |
45|| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`), in Muse Code | Its diagnosis, choice of target, kernels, and session transcripts | `muse-spark/`, on the branch `muse-agent`. Commits co-authored by "Muse Spark". |
46|| **Others, before the event** | vLLM, vllm-metal, mlx-lm, MLX, Meta's model weights | `third_party/` at pinned commits, plus the installed wheels |
47|
48|Git hooks refuse commits that mix the two, and `tools/provenance_check.py` audits the whole history. [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md) gives the details and the commands to check them.
49|
50|## Layout
51|
52|```
53|PROVENANCE.md         who made what, and how to check it
54|claude/               everything Claude Code wrote, apart from this README
55|claude/GLOSSARY.md    shared vocabulary
56|claude/adr/           decisions and why
57|claude/benchmark/     baseline benchmark write-up: findings, every measurement, method
58|claude/findings/      where a decode step's time goes, and the fixes it suggests
59|muse-spark/           Muse Spark's work: its diagnosis, strategy, kernels and session transcripts (branch muse-agent)
60|.agents/skills/       the round skill Muse Spark follows in Muse Code (written by Claude)
61|third_party/          pinned submodules: vllm-metal and mlx-lm (forks, where changes go), vLLM v0.32.0 (read-only)
62|bench/                benchmark sweep, roofline calculation, port correctness check
63|bench/micro/          microbenchmarks of a decode step's parts
64|bench/grader/         the independent grader for Muse Spark's kernels
65|tools/                provenance hooks and audit; the Muse Spark launcher
66|results/runs/         every benchmark run, committed
67|results/traces/       Metal GPU traces (large, not committed)
68|```
69|
70|## Setup
71|
72|Requirements: Apple Silicon, macOS 15 or later, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and Hugging Face access to `facebook/MobileMoE-S-SFT`. Full Xcode 26.2 or later is only needed to record GPU counters (`bench/micro/gpu_counters.py`), open GPU traces and rebuild vllm-metal's kernels.
73|
74|```bash
75|git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/surucuonur/meta-hackathon.git
76|cd meta-hackathon
77|uv venv .venv --python-preference only-managed --python cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64 --seed
78|source .venv/bin/activate
79|uv pip install "https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/download/v0.32.0/vllm-0.32.0%2Bcpu-cp38-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl"
80|uv pip install "https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-metal/releases/download/v0.32.0.dev20261028121433/vllm_metal-0.32.0.dev20261028121433-cp312-cp312-macosx_15_0_arm64.whl"
81|uv pip install --no-deps -e third_party/mlx-lm
82|uv pip install -e bench/steplog matplotlib
83|```
84|
85|Python must be native arm64. An Intel Python running under Rosetta can't install these wheels, so `--python` forces uv's own arm64 build. The vllm-metal wheel is the prebuilt release of the commit pinned in `third_party/vllm-metal`. The editable `mlx-lm` install is the fork where the MobileMoE port lives.
86|
87|vllm-metal's own tools (for example `tools/check_parity.py`) import the submodule's source, which has no compiled kernels until it is built with Xcode. Until then, copy them from the wheel (same commit; the files are git-ignored in the submodule):
88|
89|```bash
90|W=.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm_metal
91|for f in $(cd $W && ls metal/*.metallib metal/_paged_ops.* pytorch_backend/_mps_ops.*so pytorch_backend/_mps_ops.torch-version); do
92|  cp "$W/$f" "third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/$f"
93|done
94|```
95|
96|`.env` is not committed. It holds `MODEL_API_KEY` for Muse Spark and `HUGGINGFACE_API_KEY` for downloading the gated model; the scripts pass the second one to Hugging Face tools as `HF_TOKEN`.
97|
98|The int4 model is converted to MLX's format once. The serving copy has bfloat16 scales; the float32 copy keeps the scales exact for the correctness check. Both go to `models/` (git-ignored):
99|
100|```bash
101|.venv/bin/python bench/convert_qat.py                   # needs HF_TOKEN for the first download
102|.venv/bin/python bench/convert_qat.py --dtype float32
103|```
104|
105|### Port check
106|
107|No inference engine supported MobileMoE, so it is ported to mlx_lm (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`). `bench/check_port.py` compares the port with Meta's PyTorch code on fixed prompts. Meta's code needs transformers 4.57 and mlx-lm needs 5.7 or newer, so the reference runs in a second environment:
108|
109|```bash
110|uv venv .venv-ref --python-preference only-managed --python cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64 --seed
111|uv pip install --python .venv-ref/bin/python torch "transformers==4.57.6" numpy jinja2 safetensors
112|for dtype in float32 bfloat16; do
113|  .venv-ref/bin/python bench/check_port.py ref --dtype $dtype
114|  .venv/bin/python bench/check_port.py mlx --dtype $dtype
115|done
116|```
117|
118|float32 is the correctness gate: same greedy tokens, same top-1 token at every position, and logits within 0.01. bfloat16 is a sanity gate: the port's error against the exact answer must stay within 1.5x of the reference's own bfloat16 error. Summaries go to `results/port/`. For the int4 model, the same steps run with `--model facebook/MobileMoE-S-QAT` and the converted copies (commands in `bench/check_port.py`).
119|
120|| Model | float32 gate | bfloat16 gate (worst error ratio) |
121||---|---|---|
122|| MobileMoE-S-SFT | PASS, logits within 0.0001 | PASS (1.18) |
123|| MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4) | PASS, logits within 0.0001 | PASS (1.43; the bfloat16 scales round each group of 32 weights together) |
124|
125|A second check confirms that serving through vLLM gives the same tokens as plain mlx_lm, because vllm-metal runs its own attention code instead of the port's: 0 failures in 80 requests for both models ([SFT](results/port/MobileMoE-S-SFT-serving-parity.md), [QAT](results/port/MobileMoE-S-QAT-serving-parity.md)).
126|
127|## Baseline results
128|
129|The unmodified engine (vLLM 0.32.0, vllm-metal 0.32.0.dev20261028121433, mlx 0.32.4) serving MobileMoE-S-QAT on an M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 16 GB, macOS 15.7.4, on AC power). Random-token prompts of 128 or 1,024 tokens, 256 generated tokens each, 1 to 32 requests in flight. Every point ran 3 times in shuffled order. All files are in [results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/](results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/), with the [full table](results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/summary.md). The full write-up, with every measurement and how it was made, is in [claude/benchmark/](claude/benchmark/).
130|
131|![Roofline and step-time breakdown](results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/roofline.png)
132|
133|Steady decode steps only (no prompt tokens in the step). "MB read" is what the step must read: the weights of the experts its rows use, the rest of the weights, and the rows' attention cache. "Lower bound" is the step time at peak bandwidth or peak compute, whichever is slower.
134|
135|| Prompt | Requests | Step ms | Decode tok/s | Distinct experts / layer | MB read | GB/s (% of peak) | CPU ms in step submit | Lower bound ms |
136||---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
137|| 128 | 1 | 5.5 | 182 | 4.0 | 179 | 32.6 (16%) | 4.7 | 0.9 |
138|| 128 | 4 | 9.7 | 414 | 12.6 | 290 | 30.0 (15%) | 5.2 | 1.5 |
139|| 128 | 16 | 21.3 | 753 | 29.1 | 535 | 25.2 (13%) | 6.5 | 2.7 |
140|| 128 | 32 | 30.0 | 1,065 | 38.2 | 720 | 24.0 (12%) | 6.9 | 3.6 |
141|| 1024 | 1 | 5.9 | 169 | 4.0 | 197 | 33.3 (17%) | 5.0 | 1.0 |
142|| 1024 | 32 | 40.0 | 800 | 32.9 | 1,248 | 31.2 (16%) | 7.3 | 6.2 |
143|
144|What the data shows:
145|
146|- **No step is bandwidth-bound or compute-bound.** Achieved bandwidth stays at 24–34 GB/s for every setting, and each step takes 6–8 times its lower bound. In the terms of [GLOSSARY.md](claude/GLOSSARY.md), the baseline is overhead-bound everywhere.
147|- **Batching helps, but each extra request costs a lot.** With 128-token prompts, 32 requests give 5.9 times the tokens per second of one request. The step grows by about 0.8 ms per request, while the bytes it must read grow by about 17 MB per request, which takes 0.09 ms at peak bandwidth.
148|- **With one request, the CPU and the GPU are both near their limit.** vllm-metal's step-submit call uses 4.7 ms of CPU time in a 5.5 ms step, so even a perfect GPU would leave the step near 5 ms.
149|- **With more requests, the GPU work sets the pace.** The CPU time grows only to 7 ms at 32 requests. The rest of the submit call is waiting, and macOS reports the GPU busy for 90–100% of every run. The GPU has work queued almost all the time, but that work moves only about 30 GB/s.
150|
151|Where the time goes, from microbenchmarks run after the sweep ([claude/findings/decode-bottlenecks.md](claude/findings/decode-bottlenecks.md)):
152|
153|- **Kernel count.** vLLM itself adds 7–20%, mostly in vllm-metal's attention path ([step-breakdown.md](claude/findings/step-breakdown.md)). Each step is about 870 small GPU kernels with a fixed cost each.
154|- **Expert reads.** MLX reads each expert's weights once per (token, expert) pair, because it picks its grouped kernel only from 60 rows per step.
155|- **Attention.** vllm-metal's grouped-query attention kernel doesn't support MobileMoE-S's 12/4 head layout, so the keys and values are read three times.
156|
157|The weight layout of Meta's experts is not the main cause.
158|
159|Limits of these numbers:
160|
161|- **Swapping:** the Mac swapped out 0–7,567 pages/s during runs (322 pages/s idle). One run (128-token prompts, 16 requests) was 7% slower than its repeats during the heaviest swapping; the medians above are robust to it.
162|- **Bytes:** activations are not counted, and the GPU-busy figure is macOS's device-wide counter, which says the GPU had work, not how efficiently it ran.
163|- **Prompts:** they are random tokens. Expert routing on real text may pick different numbers of distinct experts.
164|
165|Reproduce (about 35 minutes):
166|
167|```bash
168|.venv/bin/python bench/sweep.py --label baseline
169|.venv/bin/python bench/roofline.py results/runs/<date>-baseline
170|```
171|
172|`bench/steplog` is a vLLM plugin that records every engine step (requests advanced, prompt tokens, context read, time in the step-submit call); `bench/sweep.py` runs the grid against a real `vllm serve`, then repeats it once with distinct-expert counting on; `bench/roofline.py` turns the logs into the table and chart.
